sections.heading: a b s t r a c t
sections.text:
In view of the unsatisfactory utilization efficiency of the piezoelectric patches used in the conventional harvesters, this research develops a novel efficient cylinder energy harvester made of L-shaped piezoelectric coupled beams by fully using the positive piezoelectric effect of the piezoelectric patch. Due to lack of accurate theory model of the L-shaped beam, experimental research is employed to study the advantages of the developed harvester which includes a pair of stators, a rotor and a cylindrical shell. Sets of stator specimens, a rotor, and a cylindrical shell are customized and five groups of experiments are conducted. The influences of some factors on the output voltage and power from an L-shaped beam are tested and analyzed. The output power and peak-to-peak voltage at a resonance can easily reach up to $2 . 3 5 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ and $5 0 ~ \mathrm { V }$ for a piezoelectric patch with a dimension of $3 8 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 1 3 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ of an Lshaped beam in the vibration process. This research provides an ingenious and compact structure for energy harvesting from ambient vibration such as wind and its effectiveness and efficiency are validated through a series of experiments.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
In recent decades, how to transform energy from ambient environment into electricity has always been an attractive subject for researchers and engineers all over the world. Among environmental energies, vibration energy is particularly abundant and has a great application potential [1e3]. The piezoelectric ceramics has the function of reciprocal conversion between mechanical energy and electrical energy [4,5]. This inherent machine-electric coupling effect makes it widely used in sensing [6e9], actuation [10e13], and energy harvesting [14e17]. More importantly, because the energy conversion density of the piezoelectric ceramics is much higher than that of the electromagnetic conversion, piezoelectric energy harvesting technologies have become the optimal method to absorb ambient vibration energy [18,19], such as the piezoelectric shoes [20,21], the piezoelectric floor tiles [22] and the piezoelectric devices used in energy harvesting from roads and bridges [23e26].

Piezoelectric energy harvesting devices usually are the piezoelectric coupled cantilever structures which can generate useable power in a slight excitation [27e30]. Na et al. [31], Wu et al. [32], and Zhang et al. [33] proposed their respective wind energy harvester made of one or more piezoelectric coupled cantilevers. Ghayesh et al. [34], Thein et al. [35], Basutkar [36], and Wu et al. [37] studied the bimorph piezoelectric coupled cantilever harvesters in different aspect. Kurmendra et al. [38] proposed a rectangular-cantilever MEMS (Microelectro Mechanical Systems) which can be used as a RF(Ratio Frequency) sensor bonded on vibrators and oscillators. Zhang et al. [39] and Stamatellou et al. [40] investigated the flow-induced vibration harvester of a piezoelectric coupled cantilever by their respective method. Noras and Vo [41] designed and built a flexible piezoelectric coupled cantilever structure. Ong et al. [42], Li et al. [43], and Fu et al. [44] developed their respective piezoelectric cantilever harvesters with different superiority for harvesting the low-frequency vibration energy. Although the harvesters aforementioned are effective in harvesting environmental vibration energy, their output voltage/power densities are unsatisfactory for the uneven strain of the piezoelectric material in the vibration process.

In order to improve the output voltage/power density of the piezoelectric harvester, some researchers attempted to design triangular piezoelectric coupled cantilever harvester, which has a comparative uniform surface strain compared to that of the uniform cantilever in the vibration process, to increase the energy harvesting efficiency [45]. Keshmiri et al. [46] proposed a new type of nonlinear cone-shaped piezoelectric cantilever beam which has a generation efficiency of 19.76 times higher than that of the traditional uniform cantilever generator. Xie et al. [47] developed a tapered-shape piezoelectric energy harvesting structure, later on, designed two piezoelectric devices by fixing the tapered-shape structures in boxes for harvesting ocean wave energy [48,49]. Zhang et al. [50] presented a variable cross piezoelectric coupled harvester to absorb wave energy, which is 2.4 times more efficient than the uniform cantilever harvester. Mehraeen et al. [51] gave a field test of a proposed tapered beam and found tapered cantilever beams are more effective in generating a uniform strain profile over rectangular and trapezoidal beams.

As mentioned above, the tapered cantilever harvesters can improve the energy harvesting efficiency for the relatively uniform surface strain of their piezoelectric patches, however the surface strain still has strain concentration near the fixed end of the tapered cantilever harvester in the vibration process. In order to further improve the energy harvesting efficiency, Hu et al. [52] developed a harvester made of a series of U-shaped piezoelectric beams excited by the magnetic force, which has a considerable energy harvesting efficiency for the complete uniform surface strain in the piezoelectric coupled segment (PCS) in the vibration process. However, this research was conducted only by theoretical analysis and simulation and was not validated by experiments. In view of this, based on L-shaped piezoelectric coupled beam which has an ideal uniform surface strain in the PCS, a new energy harvester is developed. In order to verify the effectiveness of the new proposed harvester, its energy harvesting performance is experimentally studied by changing the design parameters of the harvester.

Fig. 1(a) shows the structure of an L-shaped piezoelectric coupled beam, which includes a piezoelectric coupled segment (PCS) with a piezoelectric patch bonded on the substrate surface and an excitation segment with a magnet brick embedded in the groove of its free end. sections.heading: 3. Experimental study
sections.text:
In this section, five sets of stator specimens, a rotor, and a cylindrical shell are customized. The stator specimens of 1#-5# shown in Fig. 4 are composed of substrates made of Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) material and piezoelectric patches made of PZT4 ceramics. The rotor is an ABS disc fixed on a rotation shaft made of stainless steel, and the rotation disc includes magnet bricks embedded in the grooves along its edge. The cylindrical shell made of ABS has an enough thickness to install the stators and fix the shaft steadily. In these specimens, the lengths and the thicknesses of the piezoelectric patch and its substrate of the PCS of the Lshaped beam are taken as variables to study their influences on the energy harvesting performance of the harvester. The parameters of the L-shaped beams for 1#-5# specimens are revealed in Tables 2e3. The piezoelectric patches with different thickness are bonded tightly on the substrate surface of the PCS of the L-shaped beam by epoxy resin to make them have a fully uniform strain with the substrate surface of the PCS in the vibration process. In these experiments, the upper surface of the piezoelectric patch is connected by a wire as its positive electrode, while the lower surface of the piezoelectric patch is led out by a copper coil as its negative electrode to ensure the tight stick between the piezoelectric patch surface and the substrate surface. The experimental setting is shown as Fig. 5, in which the rotor is driven by an optical shaft motor (2IK6A-A, $0 { - } 1 2 0 \operatorname { H z }$ , $\pm 0 . 9 \%$ ) with a speed adjuster. Moreover, the output voltage of the piezoelectric signal collector (SC-HY-PZT-2.0, $\pm 5 0 \mathrm { ~ V } , \pm 1 \% )$ is collected and recorded by the computer. The resistance box (ZX1M, 0e1000 KU, $\pm 0 . 1 \% )$ is used to adjust the load resistance to find the optimal value to achieve the maximum output power. In the following, five groups of experiments are conducted. The influences of the excitation frequency and the distance of d, the substrate thickness in PCS, the length of the PCS, the thickness of the PZT4 patch, and the load resistance on the output voltage and power from an L-shaped beam are analyzed and discussed. ![](images/c9932eec8279ed3c48c5ccbaaff7ad240775cfde296f59b612e16c8f30a646cb.jpg) Fig. 4. sections.heading: 4. Results and analysis
sections.text: Based on the experiments designed above, the influences of some important factors, including the excitation frequency of the Lshaped beam, the distance $d$ between two excitation magnet bricks on the stator and the rotor, the length $L _ { 1 } ,$ the substrate thickness $t _ { 1 } ,$ and the piezoelectric patch thickness $t _ { p }$ in the PCS of the L-shaped beam, on the energy harvesting performance of the harvester will be discussed. In the experiment process, the output voltages are measured by the piezoelectric signal collector (SC-HY-PZT-2.0, $\pm 5 0 \mathrm { V } , \pm 1 \% )$ and reported by the computer, the output powers are directly computed by using the formula of $\scriptstyle P = U ^ { 2 } / R .$ . Therefore, the output electric parameters from the harvester are reliable because the experiment process is controlled by the instruments and the computer which have an ideal accuracy, and there is no error from person behavior. In addition, it is worth mentioning that the ABS material is adopted to manufacture the stators mainly because it has a small Young’s modulus, which makes the PZT4 patch bonded on the surface of the ABS L-shaped beam have a big surface strain in the vibration process.

sections.heading: 4.1. Effect of the excitation frequency and the distance of d
sections.text:
By adjusting the distance of d, a series of experiments are conducted, the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of $1 \# { - } 5 \#$ stators bonded piezoelectric patches with same thickness of $t _ { p } = 1$ mm are tested in the action of magnet excitation force with changing excitation frequency. The experimental results are displayed in Fig. 6. From Fig. 6, it can be found that the peak-to-peak voltages from the L-shaped beams appear two resonant peaks with the increase of the excitation frequency from $2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . And the maximum peak-to-peak voltages happen at the 1st (not the 2nd) resonance because the PCS just has a uniform strain in the vibration process when its excitation frequency is less than and near its 1st natural frequency. From Fig. 6(a)e(b), it can be seen the 1st and the 2nd resonant frequencies of the L-shaped beam of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator are less than the corresponding ones of 1# stator because the thinner substrate thickness in the PCS of 2# stator, which leads to the smaller natural frequencies of the L-shaped beam of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator for its smaller flexural rigidity shown as Eq. (1) as bellow. From Fig. 6(c)e(d), it can be found that the 1st and the 2nd resonant frequencies of the L-shaped beam of 4# stator are all larger than those from 3# stator for the shorter PCS of 4# stator, the reason also can be indicated from Eq. (1). Similarly, from Fig. 6(d)e(e), it can be observed that the 1st and the 2nd resonant frequencies of the Lshaped beam from 5# stator are all less than those from 4# stator because the thinner PCS substrate of $5 \#$ stator causes the smaller flexural rigidity of its L-shaped beam, which can be explained by Eq. (1).

sections.heading: 4.2.1. Comparison of peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 1#- 2# stators
sections.text:
In order to study the influence of the substrate thickness in PCS of the L-shaped beam on its energy harvesting performance, the experimental results of the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of $^ { 1 \# - 2 \# }$ stators are taken out for a comparison. In this experiment, the parameters for an L-shaped beam of $^ { 1 \# }$ and $^ { 2 \# }$ stators are displayed in Tables 2e3

The curves of the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of $^ { 1 \# }$ and $^ { 2 \# }$ stators along the excitation frequencies when the distance of $d$ is $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , $3 \mathrm { m m }$ , $4 \mathrm { m m }$ , $5 \mathrm { m m }$ , and $6 \mathrm { { m m } }$ are displayed in Fig. 7(a), (b), (c), (d), and (e), respectively. From Fig. 7, it can be seen that the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 1# and $^ { 2 \# }$ stators just have one obvious peak with the increase of the excitation frequency from $2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , which is because the PCS has a uniform strain in the vibration process just when the excitation frequency is less than and near the 1st natural frequency of the L-shaped beam of the stators. It also can be observed that the peak-to-peak voltages from $^ { 2 \# }$ stator’s L-shaped beam are larger than the corresponding ones from 1# stator when $d$ is in the range of $2 \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \mathrm { m m }$ . The reason is, in the vibration process, the thinner PCS substrate of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator causes the smaller flexural rigidity of the L-shaped beam and the corresponding bigger stress in its PZT4 patch, which can be explained by Eqs. (2)e(5).

And the peak-to-peak voltages from that of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator at the 1st resonant frequency of $2 5 \mathrm { H z }$ are 68 V, 64 V, 60 V, 54 V and $4 0 \mathrm { V }$ corresponding to the distance $d$ of $2 \mathrm { m m } , 3 \mathrm { m m } , 4 \mathrm { m m } , 5 \mathrm { m m }$ , and $6 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. Besides, it also can be observed that the peak-to-peak voltage densities from a PZT4 patch of $^ { 1 \# }$ and $^ { 2 \# }$ stators decrease with the increase of the distance of $d$ , for example, the peak-to-peak voltage densities decrease from $0 . 0 4 6 \mathrm { \ V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { \bar { 3 } }$ to $0 . 0 2 \dot { 5 } \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { \dot { 3 } }$ for 1# stator and from $0 . 0 9 9 \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ to $0 . 0 5 8 \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ for $^ { 2 \# }$ stator when the distance $d$ increases from $2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ to $6 \mathrm { m m }$ . This phenomenon is because the increase of the distance of d causes the decrease of the excitation magnet force, which leads to the decreases of the voltage and the voltage density shown as Eqs.(5)e(6). Notably, the peak-to-peak voltage densities from a PZT4 patch of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator are larger than the corresponding ones of 1# stator for any distance $d$ of $2 \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \mathrm { m m }$ , such as $d = 2 { \mathrm { m m } }$ , the peak-to-peak voltage density from 2# stator is $0 . 0 5 3 \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ higher than that from $^ { 1 \# }$ stator. This is because the thinner PCS substrate of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator leads to the bigger voltage density which can be explained by Eq. (6). The phenomenon above indicates that a thinner substrate in PCS and a smaller distance of $d$ are beneficial to improve the output voltage and voltage density of an L-shaped beam of the stators.

sections.heading: 4.2.2. Comparison of peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 4#-5# stators
sections.text:
In order to further study the influence of the substrate thickness in PCS of an L-shaped beam on the peak-to-peak voltage and voltage density from a PZT4 patch of PCS, the experimental results from the L-shaped beam of $4 \# { - } 5 \#$ stators are taken out to analyze. The parameters of $4 \# { - } 5 \#$ stators are shown in Tables 2e3 From Fig. 8 it can be observed that the peak-to-peak voltages from an Lshaped beam of 4#-5# stators all have two peaks along the increase of the excitation frequency from $2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . The peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 4# stator at its 1st resonant frequency of $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ are 35 V, 29 V, 26 V, 22 V and $1 8 \mathrm { V }$ corresponding to the distance $d$ of $2 \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. And the peak peakto-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of $5 \#$ stator at its 1st resonant frequency of $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ are $6 7 \mathrm { V } , 6 0 \mathrm { V } , 5 4 \mathrm { V } , 4 7 \mathrm { V }$ and $3 9 \mathrm { V }$ at $d$ of $2 \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. These data indicates that the peakto-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 5# stator are basically larger than the corresponding ones of 4# stator for any distance in the range of $2 \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \mathrm { m m }$ and any excitation frequency from $2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . This results once again show that a thinner substrate in PCS is beneficial to output a higher voltage. At the same time, it can be found that the peak-to-peak voltages from $4 \# { - } 5 \#$ stators are basically same as the corresponding values from 1#-2# stators which can be seen from 4.2.1. This phenomenon indicates that the increase of the PCS length cannot improve the output voltage from an L-shaped beam because the PCS length $\left( L _ { 1 } \right)$ and the PZT4 patch capacitance (C) change almost as a same scale, which can be explained by Eq. (5).

Besides, based on the experimental results, it can be observed that the peak-to-peak voltage densities from an L-shaped beam of #4-#5 stators decrease from $0 . 0 7 1 \ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ to $0 . 0 3 6 \ \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ and from $0 . 1 3 6 ~ \mathrm { V / m m ^ { 3 } }$ to $0 . 0 7 9 \ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ with the increase of $d$ from $2 \mathrm { m m }$ to $6 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. When the distance of $d$ is $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , the peak-to-peak voltage density from an L-shaped beam of $5 \#$ stator is $\mathsf { \bar { 0 . 0 6 5 \ v / m m ^ { 3 } } }$ higher than that of 4# stator for the thinner PCS substrate thickness of $5 \#$ stator shown as Eq. (6). The phenomena above are caused by the same two reasons as those of $^ { 1 \# - 2 \# }$ stators. The first one is that the increase of the distance of $d$ causes the decreases of the excitation magnet force and the voltage density, the second one is the thinner PCS substrate of 5# stator leads to its bigger voltage density, which also can be explained by Eq. (6). In addition, the peak-to-peak voltage density from an L-shaped beam of 5# stator is $0 . 0 9 \ \mathrm { \bar { V } / m m ^ { 3 } }$ higher than that of $^ { 1 \# }$ stator for the shorter PCS and the smaller PZT4 patch capacitance of 5# stator, which can also be indicated by Eq. (6). The observation above shows that shorter PCS and thinner substrate are advantageous for a higher output voltage density.

sections.heading: 4.3.1. Comparison of peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 1#, 3# and 4# stators
sections.text:
In this experiment, the influence of the substrate length in the PCS of the stators on their peak-to-peak voltages is tested and discussed. The dimensions and physical parameters for 1#, 3#, and 4# stators are revealed in Tables 2e3

From Fig. 9, it can be found that the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of the stators all have two peaks in the action of the excitation with a frequency from $2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , and all show a decrease with the increase of the distance of $d$ . For 1#,3#, and 4# stators, the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam at the corresponding 1st resonant frequencies of $3 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , 40 Hz, and $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ decrease from $3 2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ to 17 V, 28 Ve15 V, and $3 4 \mathrm { V } { - } 1 8 \mathrm { V }$ along the increase of the distance $d$ from $2 ~ \textrm { m }$ to $6 ~ \mathrm { \ m m }$ , respectively.

According to the data above, it can be obtained that the 1st natural frequencies of an L-shaped beam of $^ { 1 \# , 3 \# , }$ , and $^ { 4 \# }$ stators increase as $3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , $4 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , and $6 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ because their PCS lengths decrease as $5 3 \mathrm { m m }$ , $4 3 \mathrm { m m }$ , and $3 8 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. Obviously, the shortening of the PCS would cause the increase of the natural frequency of the L-shaped beam which can be explained by Eq. (1). It also can be observed from Fig. 9 that the peak-to-peak voltages from an Lshaped beam of 1#, 3#, and 4# stators at the 1st resonance are almost same, which is because the influence of the PCS length on the output voltage from an L-shaped beam counteracts that of the PZT4 patch capacitance (see Eq. (5)), namely, just increasing the PCS length cannot improve the output voltage from an L-shaped beam of the stators.

According to the experimental results, it can be observed that the peak-to-peak voltage densities from an L-shaped beam of 1#,3#, and 4# stators decrease from $0 . 0 4 6 \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ to $\mathsf { \bar { 0 } } . 0 2 5 \mathsf { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , $0 . 0 5 ~ \mathrm { V / m m ^ { 3 } }$ to $0 . 0 2 7 ~ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ , and $0 . 0 6 9 \ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ to $0 . 0 3 6 \ \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ with the increase of $d$ from $2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ to $6 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. For the distance $d$ of $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , the peak-to-peak voltage densities from an Lshaped beam of $^ { 1 \# , 3 \# , }$ and $^ { 4 \# }$ stators are $0 . 0 4 6 ~ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ , $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { ~ V / }$ $\mathrm { m } \mathrm { { \dot { m } } } ^ { 3 }$ , and $0 . 0 6 9 \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ respectively. This indicates that the peakto-peak voltage density increase with the shortening of the PCS of the stators which causes the decrease of the PZT4 patch capacitance (C), the decrease of $C$ leads to the increase of voltage density shown as Eq. (6). Based on the discussion above, it can be concluded that with the decrease of the PCS length of the stators, their peakto-peak output voltages almost keep a constant but their output voltage densities increase.

sections.heading: 4.3.2. Comparison of peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 2# and 5# stators
sections.text:
In order to further study the influence of the PCS length on the peak-to-peak voltage, the vibration tests of $^ { 2 \# }$ and $5 \#$ stators are conducted and the experimental results from an L-shaped beam of them are compared. The parameter formation of $^ { 2 \# }$ and 5# stators can be found from Tables 2e3

According to Fig. 10, it can be observed the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of $^ { 2 \# }$ and $5 \#$ stators have two peaks in the increasing process of the excitation frequency from $2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . When the distance of $d$ is $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , $3 \mathrm { m m }$ , 4 mm, 5 mm, and $6 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , the peak-to-peak voltage from an L-shaped beam of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator happening at the 1st resonant frequency of $2 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ is $6 8 ~ \mathsf { V } .$ , 64 V, 60 V, 54 V, and $4 0 \mathrm { V }$ , respectively, and that of 5# stator at the 1st resonant frequency of $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ is 67 V, 60 V, 54 V, 47 V, and $3 9 \mathrm { V }$ , respectively. The data above shows that the 1st resonant peak-topeak voltages from an L-shaped beam of $^ { 2 \# }$ stator are almost same as those of 5# stator for any distance of $d$ because the same reason as that in 4.3.1. This phenomenon again shows the increase of the PCS length almost has no influence on the output voltage from an L-shaped beam of the stators.

Based on the experiments above it can be observed the PCS of 5# stator has a higher output voltage density compared to 4# stator. When the distance of $d$ increases from $2 \mathrm { m m }$ to $6 \mathrm { m m }$ , the peak-to-peak voltage density from an L-shaped beam of $^ { 2 \# }$ and $5 \#$ stators decrease from 0.099 $\mathsf { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ to $0 . { \overset { - } { 0 . 0 5 8 } } \ \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ and from $0 . 1 3 6 \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ to $0 . 0 7 9 \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , respectively. For d of $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , the peakto-peak voltage density of 5# stator is $\bar { 0 . 0 3 7 } \ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ higher than that for $^ { 2 \# }$ stator because the PZT4 patch of 5# stator has a smaller capacitance which can be explained by Eq. (6). This indicates that shorter PCS for this harvester is more cost-effective because it has a higher voltage density. In addition, from Figs. 9 and 10 and 4.3.1, it can be observed the peak-to-peak voltages and voltage densities from $^ { 2 \# }$ and $5 \#$ stators are much larger than those from 1#, 3#, and 4# stators, which shows that the thinner PCS substrate is an optimal scheme for a higher output voltage and voltage density.

sections.heading: 4.4. Effect of the thickness of the PZT4 patch
sections.text:

sections.heading: 4.4.1. Comparison of the peak-to-peak voltages from PZT4 patches of 3# stator
sections.text:
In this experiment, peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 3# stator, of which PZT4 patches with a thickness of $t _ { p } = 1 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ and $t _ { p } = 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ are bonded on the oppisite L-shaped beams shown as Fig. 4, are tested and discussed.

In the excitation with a frequency from $2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , the peak-to-peak voltages from PZT4 patches with thicknesses of $t _ { p } = 1 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ and $t _ { p } = 0 . 5 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ (3#2) of an L-shaped beam of $^ { 3 \# }$ stator are displayed in Fig. 11(a)e(b), in which each peak-to-peak voltage curve has two obvious peaks corresponding to the 1st and 2nd resonances. From Fig. 11, it can be seen the peak-to-peak voltages from an L-shaped beam of 3# stator with a PZT4 patch of $t _ { p } = 1 \mathrm { m m }$ (3#1) at the 1st resonant frequency of $4 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ are 28 V, 26 V, $2 2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ and $1 5 \mathrm { V }$ corresponding to $d$ of $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , 3 mm, 4 mm, 5 mm and $6 \mathrm { { m m } }$ , respectively, and for the PZT4 patch of $t _ { p } = 0 . 5 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ (3#2), the peak-to-peak voltages at the 1st resonant frequency of $3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ are 21 V, 19 V, 16 V, 15 V and $1 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ when the distance $d$ increases from $2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ to $6 \mathrm { m m }$ in an increment of $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. Obviously, the 1st and 2nd natural frequencies of an L-shaped beam bonded 3#1 PZT4 patch are larger than those of an L-shaped beam bonded 3#2 PZT4 patch because the thicker PZT4 patch causes a bigger inertia moment of the PCS, which can be explained by Eq. (1). Besides, the peak-to-peak voltages from 3#1 PZT4 patch of $^ { 3 \# }$ stator are larger than those from 3#2 PZT4 patch along the excitation frequency from $2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ when the distance of $d$ in the range of $2 \ \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , which can be seen from Fig. 12. This can be explained by Eq. (5) for the comprehensive influences from the PZT4 patch thickness $( t _ { p } )$ and the PZT4 patch capacitance (C). The discussion above shows that the decrease of the PZT4 patch thickness can decrease the output voltage from an L-shaped beam of the stators.

According to the experimental results, it can be observed that the voltage densities from 3#1 and 3#2 PZT4 patches at their 1st resonances decrease from $0 . 0 5 ~ \mathrm { V / m m ^ { 3 } }$ to $0 . 0 2 7 ~ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ and from $0 . 0 7 5 \ \mathrm { V } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ to $0 . 0 3 9 \ \mathrm { V / m m } ^ { 3 }$ when the distance of $d$ increases from $2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ to $6 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. These data indicate that the thinner PZT4 patch bonded on the PCS of the stator usually has a bigger peak-to-peak voltage density than that of the thicker one although it has a smaller output voltage.

sections.heading: 4.4.2. Comparison of the peak-to-peak voltages from PZT4 patches of 4# stator
sections.text:

sections.heading: 4.5.2. Comparison of the output power from PZT4 patches of #5 stator
sections.text:
Continually, in order to study the influence of the PZT4 patch thickness on its maximum output power corresponding to the optimal load resistance, the experiments on the 5# stator with 5#1 and 5#2 PZT4 patches are conducted.

The output powers from 5#1 and 5#2 PZT4 patches of an Lshaped beam at its 1st resonance along the increase of the load resistance from $5 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $5 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ for $d$ of $2 \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \mathrm { m m }$ are displayed in Fig. 18. From Fig. 18, it can be found that the ouptut powers from 5#1 and 5#2 PZT4 patches all decrease with the increase of the distance of d, and the output powers from 5#2 PZT4 patch are larger than those from 5#1 PZT4 patch. Specially, the maximum powers from 5#1 PZT4 patch of $5 \#$ stator at the optimal load resistance of 311 $\mathbf { k } \Omega$ and the 1st resonant frequency of $5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ are $1 . 7 4 \mathrm { m W } , 1 . 4 0 \mathrm { m W } , 1 . 1 5 \mathrm { m W } , 0 . 8 7 \mathrm { m W } , 0 . 5 9 \mathrm { m W }$ when the distance $d$ is $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , 3 mm, $4 \mathrm { m m }$ , 5 mm, 6 mm respectively. And for 5#2 PZT4 patch bonded on an L-shaped beam of 5# stator, its maximum powers at the optimal load resistance of $3 3 3 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and the 1st resonant frequency of $4 0 \ H z$ are $2 . 3 5 \mathrm { m W } , 1 . 9 1 \mathrm { m W } , 1 . 5 2 \mathrm { m W } , 1 . 1 2 \mathrm { m W } ,$ $0 . 7 8 \ \mathrm { m W }$ versus the distance $d$ of $2 \ \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \ \mathrm { m m }$ respectively. This observation above indicates that the decrease of the PZT4 patch thickness $( t _ { p } )$ can obviously increase the output power of an Lshaped beam of the stators which can be explained by Eqs. (7) and (8). In addition, based on the data above, it can be obtained the power densities from 5#1 PZT4 patch of an L-shaped beam at the optimal load resistance and the 1st resonant frequency are 3.52 $\mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , $2 . 8 3 ~ \mathrm { \mu W / m m } ^ { 3 }$ , $2 . 3 3 \mathrm { \textrm { \textmu W / m m } } ^ { 3 }$ , $. 7 6 ~ \mathrm { \mu W / m m } ^ { 3 }$ , 1. $1 9 ~ \mu \mathrm { w } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ with the increase of $d$ from $2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ to $6 \mathrm { m m }$ respectively. Similarly, the output power densities of 5#2 PZT4 patch at the optimal load resistance and the 1st resonant frequency are 9.51 $\mathrm { \mu } \mathrm { w } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , 7.73 $\mu \mathrm { { W } } / \mathrm { { m m } } ^ { 3 }$ , 6.15 $\mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , $4 . 5 3 \mathrm { ^ { - } \mu W / m m ^ { 3 } }$ , 3.16 $\mathrm { \mu W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ corresponding to the distance $d$ of $2 \ \mathrm { m m } { - } 6 \ \mathrm { m m }$ respectively. Obviously, in this design of the stators, the L-shaped beam with 5#2 PZT4 patch has a much higher power densities than the L-shaped beam with 5#1 PZT4 patch for thinner 5#2 PZT4 patch which can be explained by Eq. (9). Through the discussion above, it can concluded that the decrease of the PZT4 patch thickness can effectively increase the output power and power density of an L-shaped beam of the stators.

sections.heading: 5. Discussion
sections.text:
The proposed harvester in this research is ingenious because three reasons as bellow: first, by circularly arranging the L-shaped piezoelectric coupled beams to make them compact and to ensure the uniform strain of their PCSs; second, by using magnet excitation to avoid the friction dissipation; third, by using the rotation disc embedded with big number of excitation magnet bricks to improve the excitation frequency. The key highlight for this harvester is that in the vibration process, the surface strain in the PCS of the beam is uniform and the utilization rate of the piezoelectric patch is improved. In addition, it is worth mentioning that the ABS material is adopted in this design to manufacture the stators mainly because it has a small Young’s modulus, which makes the PZT4 patch bonded on the surface of the ABS L-shaped beam have an obvious surface strain even in a small excitation. For example, when the distance $d$ is less than $5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ , the output power densities of 5#2 PZT4 patch are larger than the maximum output power densities from some of the conventional uniform cantilever harvesters which have uneven surface strain, such as $2 . 1 \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ [31] and $3 . 8 6 \mu \mathsf { W } /$ $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ [43]. Of course, with the decrease of the PZT4 patch thickness, the substrate thickness, and the distance $d$ (not less than $1 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ for this design), the output power density of the proposed harvester will be improved further.

![](images/56b411f497478805a20c0e9cd69aa19df60e0127fc9e9215fb10e87ab7d6f898.jpg)  
Fig. 18. The output powers from an L-shaped beam of 5# stator versus load resistance and distance of d.

However, the ABS material used in this design just has a small yield stress compared to that of steel material although it has a small Young’s modulus, which leads to the L-shaped beam just can bear a small excitation force. For this design, the distance $d$ cannot be less than $1 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ , otherwise, the pair magnet bricks will induce an enough large excitation force to wreck the L-shaped beam. In view of this, a new experiment will be conducted by replacing ABS material to be aluminum alloy or stainless steel in our next research to explore the maximum utilization rate of the piezoelectric patch in the proposed harvester.
